1.pericope_label: The spies asked for and commanded

schools.summary: Calvin finds the care of God in the arrangement, since drawing all twelve from one tribe would have left their fidelity open to suspicion and a tribe passed over free to object that the messengers were chosen in contempt of it, while chief men were required because obscure men are easily discredited; he reads the roll that follows as a monument of ignominy rather than a record, two excepted, and holds that Moses named the son of Nun in the spirit of prophecy. Gill says the scheme was of the people's own devising and that God rather permitted than approved it, giving Jarchi's paraphrase of the answer.

Henry calls the request the fruit of unbelief, since they would not take God's word that the land was good and had a better opinion of their own politics than of God's wisdom, and thinks it absurd to spy out a land God had already spied out for them; he sets Oshea, a prayer for salvation, against Joshua, a promise of it, and observes that the quality of the men chosen made the evil report the more believed.
Clarke notes that these twelve were not the tribal princes of the census, the names being different; Wesley traces the request to diffidence of the promise.

Ellicott denies any inconsistency between this account and Deuteronomy, since it would be wholly unlike Moses to act in a matter of such weight without seeking direction, and warns that the command no more proves the errand was God's own than the later command to Balaam proved that God approved his journey; Keil and Delitzsch set out the errand from Kadesh in the desert of Paran, to explore the way in and the nature of the land, its cities and its population.

debates.question: Did the sending of the spies come from God or from the people?

sides.position: from the people, out of unbelief; God permitted rather than approved it, and let them walk in their own counsels
the command was real, but no more implies God ordained the errand than his command to Balaam implied he approved that journey

themes: send thou men to search the land
one man of every tribe
a ruler among them
why the names are recorded

4.pericope_label: The twelve named, and Oshea called Joshua

schools.summary: Gill observes that the list is summed up again at the close so that the names may be marked, standing as they do to the disgrace of the greater number and to the honour of two.

Clarke pauses at Sethur only to dismiss what has been built on it, since the name means hidden and its letters add to six hundred and sixty-six, and then asks what use such expositions can be to any subject of history or theology; Wesley notices that Joseph's name, elsewhere given to Ephraim, here stands for Manasseh, and wonders whether it is set down to aggravate the sin of a ruler who so basely degenerated from his ancestor, and reads the change of Joshua's name as a prophecy both of his succession to Moses and of the success of his arms.

Ellicott reports the conjecture that Caleb was of foreign origin, since he is thrice called the Kenizzite and the Kenizzites appear among the Canaanite tribes, but thinks it rests on insufficient grounds; he suspects a displacement of the text at Ephraim, since Zebulun would naturally have followed Issachar, and will not have the change of Joshua's name fixed to this occasion, since it may have been made earlier and only confirmed now, as with Israel and Bethel, or used proleptically in the earlier books.

sides.position: not necessarily here — the change may be earlier and only confirmed now, or the name used proleptically in Exodus and Numbers
some hold the change followed the victory over Amalek

themes: the twelve rulers named
Caleb the Kenizzite
Oshea called Jehoshua
the name that is Jesus

17.pericope_label: The charge given to the spies

schools.summary: Calvin explains why the questions hang together, since a barren country cannot support a large population and the healthfulness of a place may be inferred from the vigour of those living in it, and thinks the main point was to let the pleasantness of the land allure them to go up and take it, though God may also have meant them forewarned of strong enemies lest the sudden sight dismay them; Gill adds the questions of air and climate and water, which he says stood first in intention though they come second in the text.

Clarke divides the charge into its parts, what sort of country it is and how situated, and whether the people are healthy and hardy or little and weak; Wesley explains why they began in the south, it being the nearest part and the worst, dry and desert, so that they could pass through with least notice taken of them, and notes that unwalled villages lie exposed to an enemy as tents do.

Ellicott renders the first direction not southward but by the Negeb, the transition from desert to cultivated land, prefers inspect to see, the very word used of the priest inspecting a leper, prefers camps to tents, and observes that the season suited the errand, since the first grapes ripen in Palestine as early as July; Keil and Delitzsch report how far the men actually went, from the desert of Zin at the northern edge of Paran to Rehob near Hamath.

themes: go up by the Negeb and into the mountain
whether the people be strong or weak
in tents or in strong holds
whether the land be fat or lean

21.pericope_label: The circuit of the land, and Hebron

schools.summary: Calvin thinks their industry deserves its credit, since in so short a time they examined the whole country and did it in the hottest part of the year, and answers the opinion that Anak is no proper name but a word for giants from the close of the chapter, where Anak plainly is a man whose sons were of excessive height; he also draws from the comparison with Zoan that Canaan was well peopled immediately after the flood, which argues its fertility, since men free to settle where they chose would not have preferred it had the neighbouring countries been richer. Gill explains why the text says they ascended, the hill country being reached again on the return.

Henry supposes they did not travel as one body, lest they be suspected and taken up, but passed in companies as wayfaring men, and finds Hebron chosen because the field of Machpelah lay near it, where the patriarchs' bodies kept possession of the land for their posterity — so that where they looked for their greatest encouragement they met their greatest discouragement, the giants holding the ground against them where the dead fathers held it for them.

Clarke distinguishes this desert of Zin from the Sin of the earlier march and traces the whole circuit, up nearly along the Jordan to Rehob and back through the middle of the country by the borders of the Sidonians and Philistines; he identifies Zoan with Tanis and reports both the opinion that the note was added to humble a people who boasted the highest antiquity of any and the suggestion that it was a marginal gloss, which he answers from the manuscripts. Wesley names Caleb as the one who went up to Hebron, and makes the presence of the giants an argument for the land, since they had chosen it to live in.

Ellicott points out that the Hebrew has he came, not they came, so that the twelve may not have kept together, and reports that some take Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai for tribes rather than men, though the same men may have been living fifty years later when Caleb drove them out; Keil and Delitzsch confirm what would be reported of the fruit, bunches of eight, ten and twelve pounds being still met with in Palestine.

debates.question: Are Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai men or clans, and is Anak a name?

sides.position: some take the three for tribes, though they may equally be men still living fifty years later
Anak is the proper name of a man, as the close of the chapter shows, and these three were formidable for their stature

themes: from the wilderness of Zin unto Rehob
Hebron and the children of Anak
built seven years before Zoan
the field of Machpelah near by

23.pericope_label: The cluster of Eshcol, and the return

schools.summary: Calvin fastens on the single word that turns the report, since everything the ten said was true and at first sight blameless, yet they spoke of the difficulties in terms designed to turn the people back; they had not openly lied but were wanting in sincerity, laying a foundation of good faith the better to deceive, from which he warns that crafty men gain nothing with God by covering deceit with tortuous prevarications. Gill notes that the valley cannot have borne the name at the time, being called Eshcol afterwards in memory of what was done there.

Clarke gathers travellers' reports of enormous bunches from Africa, Rhodes and Damascus, and adds the point that gives the story its force, that the Egyptian grape is small and was the only grape the Israelites knew; Wesley wonders at the forty days from the other side, that the people had patience to wait so long when they were ready to enter and had every assurance divine power could give, choosing to be held in suspense by their own counsels rather than rest on the promise.

Ellicott is the more restrained about the cluster, putting the largest ordinarily grown at ten or twelve pounds, though he cites a Syrian bunch of nineteen pounds raised in England and carried twenty miles upon a staff by four labourers, and he notes that the verse explains why Israel called the valley Eshcol without settling whether it had carried the name already; Keil and Delitzsch give the shape of the report, the fertility granted and the fruit produced, and then the single word on which it turned.

debates.question: Why was the cluster carried on a staff between two men?

sides.position: less for the weight than to bring the fruit home unbruised, as a fair specimen
either for the weight, considering the length of the way, or for keeping it whole

themes: the branch with one cluster of grapes
borne between two upon a staff
the brook Eshcol
they returned after forty days

26.pericope_label: The report brought back to Kadesh

schools.summary: Gill notes that the men went straight to Moses and Aaron before their own tents, puts the objection as the spies meant it — that however desirable the country, the strength of its inhabitants lay against all hope of possessing it — and observes that the Amalekites were named though they were no Canaanites, being neighbours to them and enemies to Israel since Rephidim.

Henry marks where the account divides and thinks the majority report a judgment as much as a failure, since it is a righteous thing with God to give men up to strong delusions who will not receive his truth in the love of it; he turns the spies' own concession against them, that even out of the mouth of adversaries God will be glorified, and reads the geography the opposite way from Wesley, the dispersion of the Canaanites meaning they could neither soon get together nor long keep together, while the overgrown stature of the giants would only make them the better mark.

Clarke finds it astonishing that men so dastardly should have had courage to risk their persons in searching the land, and supposes that though destitute of valour they had a sufficiency of cunning; Wesley takes the closing list as a catalogue of obstacles arranged by compass point, the Amalekites holding the south where Israel must enter and the salt sea guarding the eastern approach.

Ellicott sets out the rival identifications of Kadesh and observes that the spies took up the very words of the promise at the bush before undoing them with the fortified cities and the gigantic inhabitants; Keil and Delitzsch note that tidings of this character were bound to excite the people.

debates.question: What does the dispersion of the Canaanites prove?

sides.position: that every approach was guarded — Amalek in the south, the hill country in the south-east, the Canaanites along the salt sea
the opposite — being scattered they could neither soon get together nor long keep together, so the spies were merely cowardly

themes: surely it floweth with milk and honey
nevertheless the people be strong
the cities are walled and very great
where the nations dwelt

schools.summary: Calvin reasons from the word stilled that there would have been no need to restrain violence unless the contention had waxed warm, so that much was said on both sides which is passed over, and grounds Caleb's confidence on the promise, which the others never took into account; he holds that Caleb spoke for both men, Joshua being prudently silent lest a tumultuous altercation arise, and sees the honesty of Moses in preferring Caleb at the cost of his own servant's praise. Gill supposes the people were already making up to Moses with threats when Caleb signified that he had something to say.

Wesley notices that Caleb does not say let us go up and conquer it but let us go up and possess it, looking on the conquest as good as done, so that difficulties in the way of salvation vanish before a lively faith; and he sees in the answer of the ten a questioning of the power and the truth and the goodness of God, of all which they had ample testimonies.

Ellicott observes how much the narrative leaves out, since Joshua concurred with Caleb as the next chapter shows and Moses remonstrated earnestly as Deuteronomy shows, neither appearing here; Keil and Delitzsch state the contrary opinion of his companions plainly, that the going up was impossible because the people there were stronger than Israel.

outliers.note: Reads the silence about Joshua as deliberate on Moses' part, who by giving the credit to Caleb diminishes the praise due to his own minister.

themes: Caleb stilled the people before Moses
let us go up at once and possess it
we are well able to overcome it
we be not able to go up

32.pericope_label: The evil report and the giants

schools.summary: Calvin describes the change as a progress in boldness, the authors of the rebellion having begun with obscure insinuations and now throwing aside all shame, until in their falsehood they contradict themselves, having confessed the land rich and now declaring that it devours those who live in it — which he takes to mean that its cultivation was difficult and full of inconvenience; he would also mend the last clause by inverting it, so that as grasshoppers are despised in our eyes, so were they looked down upon by the giants for their lowness of stature. Gill marks the change of language as evidence of their want of integrity, and notes that they had seen the giants at Hebron only, and there were three.

Clarke does not doubt they saw a robust race of great stature, since neither Joshua nor Caleb denies it, but will not have a nation twelve or fourteen feet high, reporting from his own neighbourhood two brothers above seven feet and a third of eight feet six, and suggesting that the comparison was unfair on Israel's side, their growth having probably been cramped by the long servitude in Egypt; he ends by turning the report into a warning against preachers who allow the land is good and then pronounce the enemy unconquerable. Wesley guesses that the spies had seen many funerals, and adds that if they did, the cause was the providence of God thinning the Canaanites before Israel.

Ellicott lays out three possible senses of the land that eateth up its inhabitants — scarcity, unhealthiness, or the strife of those contending for it — and inclines to the last; he notes that the word for giants is the nephilim of Genesis, and denies there is any evidence that the inhabitants generally were of extraordinary size; Keil and Delitzsch reject Calvin's reading by name and hold that the land was an apple of discord, wasting its people because the surrounding nations strove for so fruitful and well-placed a country.

debates.question: What did the spies mean by a land that eateth up its inhabitants?

sides.position: that its cultivation was difficult and full of inconvenience
not that at all — the land was an apple of discord, wasting its people through the strife of the nations contending for it
that the air was unwholesome, guessed from the many funerals they saw

themes: a land that eateth up the inhabitants
men of a great stature
the sons of Anak
we were in our own sight as grasshoppers
